claims.text: Plasma nitriding Ti6Al4V at approximately 500°C in a controlled nitrogen-hydrogen atmosphere will produce a uniform titanium-nitride-enriched surface layer.
The nitrided surface layer will be hardened relative to untreated Ti6Al4V.
Plasma nitriding will increase Ti6Al4V surface hardness by at least 40%.
Plasma nitriding will improve the wear resistance of Ti6Al4V relative to an untreated surface.
Plasma nitriding will improve the corrosion resistance of Ti6Al4V relative to an untreated surface.
Real-time monitoring can control nitriding depth and nitride-layer growth during the proposed treatment.
Controlled plasma nitriding can form a nitride layer a few microns thick without altering the bulk properties of Ti6Al4V.
Precise control of temperature, gas composition, and treatment time will prevent excessive nitrogen diffusion and resulting embrittlement.
The treatment produces a titanium-nitride-enriched layer of controlled thickness.
The titanium-nitride-enriched layer has improved adhesion to the underlying Ti6Al4V substrate.
Nitrogen diffuses into Ti6Al4V and reacts to form titanium nitride phases.
Titanium nitride phases increase surface hardness.
The nitride layer acts as a barrier to corrosive agents.
Controlled nitrogen diffusion can preserve the alloy's toughness while retaining an effective surface layer.
Nitrided Ti6Al4V will have lower wear rates than untreated Ti6Al4V in accelerated testing.
Nitrided Ti6Al4V will have improved resistance to localized corrosion under accelerated testing.
The improvements will persist under service conditions typical of aerospace and biomedical applications if service temperatures do not substantially exceed the treatment temperature.
The magnitude of improvement may vary with processing conditions and alloy composition.
Increased hardness from plasma nitriding may be accompanied by embrittlement.
Failure to achieve a 40% hardness increase, significant wear and corrosion reductions, or avoidance of cracking and embrittlement would falsify the hypothesis.
